text.p: The head of French military aircraft maker Dassault Aviation said on Saturday he still favoured merging with state-owned Aerospatiale as long as the new group were privatised immediately.
But he said privately-owned Dassault could accept the state keeping a stake as big as 49 percent in the new merged entity.

Dassault Aviation was scheduled to merge with Aerospatiale this year as part of a French aerospace industry restructuring launched by President Jacques Chirac in February 1996. But the election of a Socialist-led government this month has raised doubt about the deal.
The Dassault-Aerospatiale merged group would have been privatised this year under the original plan.

"I remain in favour of a merger with Aerospatiale, provided this operation occurs simultaneously with privatisation," chairman Serge Dassault, whose family owns the biggest share in the group, told a news conference at the Paris air show.
Asked what degree of private ownership would be sufficient, Dassault replied, "Fifty-one percent -- that's enough for it to be considered a private company".
The Socialist Party said during the campaign that it favoured the merger but would halt the privatisation programme begun by prior conservative governments.
The new government has not declared its position. Officials say the case is under study.

Dassault said the ball was in Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's court, as the blueprint for the new organisation had been already laid out by Dassault and Aerospatiale managers. "We're ready. It's now up to the government," he said.
Dassault vice chairman Charles Edelstenne told reporters it would be "no tragedy" if the merger did not take place.
He said the company has successful programmes with the Falcon business jets and Rafale and Mirage warplanes. But Dassault would have to find a European partner to develop the next combat plane.

Dassault has also linked up with electrical engineering and telecoms giant Alcatel Alsthom in a bid for defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, 58 percent held by the wholly state-owned Thomson SA group. The outlook for the Thomson-CSF sale has also become unclear.
"Thomson-CSF was sidelined from some European restructurings because of its status as a nationalised company. This situation risks growing worse is the status quo is maintained," Edelstenne said.

Serge Dassault said the restructuring of the U.S. aerospace industry, with the creation of Lockheed Martin and the proposed Boeing -McDonnell Douglas merger, made it imperative for the European industry to restructure.
He said France's industry risked falling back into a secondary role if it did not participate in the restructuring.
"Our partners will not accept our participation in these negotiations unless we come ... on an equal footing, which is to say as a private industry," he said.
Dassault, whose share price has been hurt by the uncertainty resulting from the change in government, agreed reluctantly to a merger with Aerospatiale.
The government's aim was to restructure France's defence sector, creating a small group of powerful players able to play an important role in the European industry's consolidation.

The merger of Aerospatiale and Dassault would form a leading European aerospace group manufacturing combat planes, business jets, helicopters, missiles and satellites. Aerospatiale is also a partner in the Airbus Industrie commercial plane consortium.
